title: Riding home
hook: sixth picture: he rides the ox home, playing the flute

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifth picture: the ox grows gentle through patient tending, until it follows without a rope. Your line: tamed. Which small practice did you return to? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-six.

Evening. A path through the fields. An ox walks slowly toward a village, and on its back sits a man who isn't holding the rope at all. He has a flute to his lips and he's playing a simple tune, the kind children sing. Sometimes he looks up at the clouds. The ox knows the way. Two pictures ago this same animal was dragging him toward the hills. Now there's nothing to hold. In the sixth oxherding picture, the hard part is over. Today: riding home.
screen: `EVENING, A PATH THROUGH THE FIELDS.` → `NO HAND ON THE ROPE.` → `A FLUTE AND THE CLOUDS.`

segments.voice: First, the struggle is over. The preface for this picture says it plainly, in paraphrase: the struggle has ended, and gain and loss no longer grip him. The rope that went taut in the fourth picture has nothing left to do. What was effort has become ease. Second, the flute. The herdsman plays country songs, the preface says, the tunes of woodcutters and children. Not a grand hymn. Nothing that needs an audience. The picture's sign of a settled mind is someone humming on the way home. That's worth noticing. In this teaching, practice that's gone deep doesn't look solemn. It looks relaxed, even a little playful. Third, he doesn't turn around. The preface adds a detail that's easy to miss: if someone calls to him, he won't look back; if someone tugs at him, he won't stop. Ease isn't the same as drifting. He's going home, and he's not distracted from it. The ox walks steadily. So does he. Fourth, home. Some Zen teachers read home as one's own original nature, the place the search set out from. The herdsman isn't traveling somewhere new. He's going back. And the preface has his eyes on the sky, not down at the path, because the path no longer needs watching. On an ordinary day, riding home can look like a practice you no longer have to force: a walk you take because you like it, a pause before meals that just happens. The verse ends, in paraphrase, by saying that whoever knows this melody needs no words.
screen: `THE STRUGGLE IS OVER.` · `A FLUTE, A COUNTRY SONG.` · `CALLED, HE DOESN'T TURN BACK.` · `GOING HOME, NOT SOMEWHERE NEW.` · then, large: `RIDING HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Let it be easy today. Sit however feels comfortable. Let the breath do what it's already doing, without steering it. If a sound arrives, let it be music. If a thought calls, you don't have to turn around; let it call. Imagine nothing, fix nothing. The ox knows the way. If a small smile shows up, let it stay. Enjoy this one easy practice. The bell holds the time.
Riding home. The sixth oxherding picture: the struggle over, the herdsman rides the ox home playing a flute, untroubled by gain and loss. Today's word.
Your line: riding home. Today, do one good habit lightly, like a tune on the way home, with no need for it to impress anyone. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Zen teachers use the sixth oxherding picture to describe a stage where practice no longer feels like a fight, and the image of the herdsman playing the flute on the ox's back also appears in Zen painting.

fork.setup: you're riding the ox home, flute in hand. someone on the roadside calls your name and tugs your sleeve. what does the sixth picture say?
options: you don't turn back; you keep riding home.
you grab the rope tight in case the ox bolts.
fork.reveal: the preface says that if called, he won't turn, and if pulled, he won't stop. the ease of the picture comes with a clear direction.

original.note: Chinese (qiniu guijia): 'riding the ox, returning home', the name of the sixth oxherding picture.

trapdoor: what you thought: riding home means the trip is over and you can stop paying attention.
what it means: practice has become easy and joyful, and still keeps its direction home.
what a scholar hears: the preface pairs the end of struggle with not turning back when called; ease and steadiness arrive together.
